item.title: Wildwood
item.description: An old friend convinced me to watch Wildwood. It is an amazing stop motion fantasy movie with so many incredible breathtaking scenes, inspired characters, beautifully mind-tickling ideas, and wonderful shots. A movie that is made for the big screen. From the studio that created Coraline. Prue is a twelve year old living in Portland. And one day her brother is being kidnapped by a murder of crows and taken to the impassable wilderness.
item.content:encoded:
An old friend convinced me to watch Wildwood. It is an amazing stop motion fantasy movie with so many incredible breathtaking scenes, inspired characters, beautifully mind-tickling ideas, and wonderful shots. A movie that is made for the big screen. From the studio that created Coraline.

Prue is a twelve year old living in Portland. And one day her brother is being kidnapped by a murder of crows and taken to the impassable wilderness. Prue follows into a world of magic.

An impressive cast, including the incomparable Angela Bassett, Tom Waits, Awkwafina, Mahershala Ali, and many others. I very strongly recommend watching it.

It is about grief, dealing with loss, struggle, about deciding whether to fight or not. And it has a big battle and at least one shocking, sudden death, both of which might be good to be aware before deciding whether to see it with smaller children.

  • Wildwood trailer

item.title: The Web of Knowledge
item.description: I thought I knew the history of Wikipedia inside and out. Then I read Giota Alevizou’s The Web of Knowledge, and I found myself honestly surprised. I learned things about Wikipedia and its role in the knowledge ecosystem that had a major impact on my career, and that I was completely unaware of. 2026 is Wikipedia’s Jubilee year, and there are a few books published retelling the history of Wikipedia. But this book goes further; it discusses the role of Wikipedia in the wider knowledge infrastructure, and it encompasses the history of (English) digital encyclopedias as a whole, covering in particular the journeys of Britannica and Encarta from the 1990s on, in addition to telling the history of Wikipedia.
item.content:encoded:
I thought I knew the history of Wikipedia inside and out. Then I read Giota Alevizou’s The Web of Knowledge, and I found myself honestly surprised. I learned things about Wikipedia and its role in the knowledge ecosystem that had a major impact on my career, and that I was completely unaware of.

2026 is Wikipedia’s Jubilee year, and there are a few books published retelling the history of Wikipedia. But this book goes further; it discusses the role of Wikipedia in the wider knowledge infrastructure, and it encompasses the history of (English) digital encyclopedias as a whole, covering in particular the journeys of Britannica and Encarta from the 1990s on, in addition to telling the history of Wikipedia.

The book starts with a foreword by Jimmy Wales, the founder of Wikipedia, in which he closes by discussing the impact AI might have on Wikipedia and the knowledge ecosystem. A timely topic that the book will pick up.

I have to admit that I had a bit of a hard time getting started with the book, particularly regarding its positioning within its theoretical frameworks. But once we started to dive into the topic, I enjoyed it quite a bit and learned a few things.

The book covers very competently the pre-history of digital encyclopedias, starting well before Diderot, covering the ‘Great Books’ of the past, the Summae, and also Otlet and Dewey and their plans to index and organize the world’s knowledge, and Nelson’s Memex, all the way to Lenat’s Cyc. Giota describes knowledge organization and the encyclopedia as parallel threads weaving through the centuries.

For me the biggest surprise was right in the origin story of Wikipedia, where both threads were tied together. A lot has been written and said about Jimmy Wales’ motivation to start an online encyclopedia, including his mother buying an encyclopedia when he was 3 years old. When Jimmy was 30 years old, in 1996, he founded Bomis, a web portal for user-generated webrings and adult content. Critics often raised the second part, but Giota’s book focuses on the first: to structure the topics of the webrings would be helpful. And what better solution for that than an encyclopedia?

This was around the same time that Yahoo started becoming the main portal to the Web, and that predecessors of DMOZ came around. Back then, Yahoo wasn’t a search portal, but a directory. Jimmy’s intuition that an encyclopedia would be a great complement or substrate to organize the webrings would prove extremely foresighted, and became one of the foundational ideas for my own career.

That’s why I was so surprised to read about it in this book. So much that I actually had to discuss this with Jimmy and he, unsurprisingly, confirmed the story.

An encyclopedia is “a systematically organized repository of knowledge”. Already in the early 20th century, Giota describes how “the encyclopedia serves as a means for the semantic structuring of (digital) information spaces”.

I want to expand on this point: Jimmy’s intuition repeatedly bore fruit in the years that followed. Ironically, to the best of my understanding he never used it to improve the organization of webrings by Bomis. In 2005, Markus Krötzsch, Max Völkel and I described the Semantic Wikipedia idea, where we suggested using Wikipedia articles as anchors for topics.

In 2007, Metaweb’s Freebase also took Wikipedia as the central semantic structure to build around, which later became the Google Knowledge Graph, considerably improving Google Search by using “things, not strings”. DBpedia, started in the same year, was also lifted off from Wikipedia and called itself a Nucleus for the Web of Open Data.

In 2012 we kicked off Wikidata to explicitly provide and entangle a machine-readable knowledge graph, firmly based on Wikipedia. Abstract Wikipedia is now a continuation of this idea, working toward a more comprehensive knowledge representation than Wikidata did, towards the more ambitious goal of allowing many more people to share knowledge across language barriers.

And although I have been working on this for more than 20 years, I did not know that using an encyclopedia as the foundational structure of the semantic space was Jimmy’s motivation all along.

But back to the book. For me, that insight alone was worth the prize of admission. And Giota doesn’t stop there. There is the widespread myth that “Wikipedia killed Britannica”, and maybe some of us know that this doesn’t align with events. Britannica was already in a steep decline when Wikipedia was founded, and the reason was Microsoft’s Encarta. And whereas I roughly knew this story, Giota really lays out the narrative with thorough evidence drawn from her own material collected over decades. She had already interviewed people involved with Britannica and Encarta in the 2000s, and used this material to lay out a fascinating story, about Britannica’s turbulent organizational history and Microsoft’s ambitions to use Encarta as the promotional vehicle to get a PC into every household: because for the price of a Britannica, you not only get an encyclopedia for your children, but you get a lot more value.

One interesting point is about finances: Giota mentions that in 1989, Britannica had $627 million in revenue. That’s almost $1.6 billion in today’s dollars.

That is roughly one order of magnitude larger than the budget of the Wikimedia Foundation. While Britannica is available only in English, Wikipedia is available in more than 300 languages.

Giota also reminds us that Encarta premiered multimedia capabilities and functionalities from which Wikipedia could still learn. But just as Encarta eroded Britannica’s financial base, Wikipedia was able to replace Encarta. Microsoft wouldn’t even put up a fight: the PC had already won the marketplace, and whether Encarta or Wikipedia was the encyclopedia, what did it matter to Microsoft?

The book outlines the history of how encyclopedic authority moved from a small group of exalted individuals to a crowd in which everyone can participate. It reminds us again how littered with accidents this history was, and how fragile the current situation is. The wide deployment and usage of AI is destabilizing a situation in more than one way, and the book outlines what we may lose if we are not careful. We must take our role as stewards of the encyclopedia seriously – I am reminded of Umberto Eco’s wonderful quote: “After all, the cultivated person’s first duty is to be always prepared to rewrite the encyclopaedia.”

Links:

  • Website about the book by King’s College London
  • A review of the book by Matthew Vetter in the International Journal of Communication

item.title: Centillion to the power of a centillion, or a googolplex?
item.content:encoded:
Computers are good with numbers.

“what’s bigger, centillition to the power of a centillion, or a googolplex?”

I am glad that Google gives me a richly sourced and well reasoned answer, linked below:

“A googolplex is vastly bigger than a centillion to the power of a centillion.”

The Math

  • Centillion: In the short scale, a centillion is 10^303 (a 1 followed by 303 zeros)
  • Centillion to the power of a centillion:
    • (10^303)^(10^303) which is roughly 10^(10^305.48).
  • Googol and Googolplex:
    • A googol is 10^100
    • A googolplex is 10^googol = 10^(10^100).

Why a Googolplex Wins

  • Centillion to the centillion power is roughly 10^(a number with about 305 digits).
  • A googolplex is 10^(a number with 101 digits), which is orders of magnitude larger.

To put it in perspective, a googolplex is so large that writing out all of its zeros in decimal form would require more paper and matter than exists in the known physical universe."

Please don’t outsource your thinking skills yet.

  • Link to answer

item.title: Patrick Stewart
item.description: When the table read of the first episode of The Next Generation happened, it was Patrick Stewart who first pronounced the name of the android Data. He enunciated a crisp T instead of the American habit of letting the letter disappear somewhere on the top of their mouth. Gene Roddenberry then set up the rule that whoever reads a name first decides on the pronunciation. Given the profound cultural impact of Star Trek this influenced the way data was pronounced, and thus much later also influenced Wikidata.
item.content:encoded:
When the table read of the first episode of The Next Generation happened, it was Patrick Stewart who first pronounced the name of the android Data. He enunciated a crisp T instead of the American habit of letting the letter disappear somewhere on the top of their mouth. Gene Roddenberry then set up the rule that whoever reads a name first decides on the pronunciation. Given the profound cultural impact of Star Trek this influenced the way data was pronounced, and thus much later also influenced Wikidata.

Captain Picard and Professor X as portrayed by Patrick Stewart embodied leadership for me, a role model since growing up. If you read up on the production of Star Trek: The Next Generation, you will learn that he also was a role model and a leader for the rest of the cast, his professionalism and conduct contributing far beyond the role he portrayed on screen. In his private life he served less of a role model, but unlike some other stars his private life sure didn’t have anywhere near the prominence in the public consciousness as the roles he portrayed have.

He’ll always be my Captain. “Make it so” is such a wonderful catchphrase, showing confidence in the capabilities of the crew, and how good communication and consensus had worked before. The scenes of Captain Picard and his leadership team sitting around the table, discussing options and coming to level headed decisions, had little counterpart on Kirk’s Enterprise. I don’t expect to get into the habit of drinking Earl Grey, hot, though.

And even though Magneto was right, Professor X exemplified the mercy and compassion I want to always aspire to. The real-world friendship with Ian McKellen provided such a fruitful interplay for the portrayal of the relationship between Professor X and Magneto: sure, both Stewart and McKellen were brilliant actors, and I have no doubt that they would have been able to bring that relationship to life on screen even if they would have despised each other off screen, but their chemistry and friendship off screen, knowing about it, just made the rivalry and friendship of the characters feel so much more vivid. I’m looking forward to seeing Patrick Stewart and Ian McKellen portray Professor X and Magneto and their relationship once again in Doomsday.

Ad Astra.

item.title: Serbia elections 2026
item.description: The election in Serbia is a win for democracy. The students’ list very intentionally ran on one message: against the Vučić government, against corruption, for accountability. They tried to avoid having a commitment on any other issue: no commitment for or against the EU, for or against Russia, for or against Lithium exports. They defied having a leader, very intentionally. They stand for basic values: for democracy, for the freedoms of speech, of press, of research and education, for a separation of powers.
item.content:encoded:
The election in Serbia is a win for democracy. The students’ list very intentionally ran on one message: against the Vučić government, against corruption, for accountability. They tried to avoid having a commitment on any other issue: no commitment for or against the EU, for or against Russia, for or against Lithium exports. They defied having a leader, very intentionally.

They stand for basic values: for democracy, for the freedoms of speech, of press, of research and education, for a separation of powers. This was enough to carry an election, fortunately, but is it enough to form a government and lead a country?

Vučić was the minister of information in the Serbia of Milošević. I wouldn’t be surprised if Vučić conceded quickly to position himself to run for president before the year is over. This isn’t over.

The hard part is starting. Rebuilding democratic structures, reinstating press freedom, gaining agreements on what to do, not just on what to be against. All the best!

P.S.: To make it clear: I am so incredibly happy Vučić conceded quickly. In my mind I imagined sonic weapons being used against an agitated crowd, police and army marching against the people, voting results being faked, tanks rolling through the streets of Niš and Belgrade, the cities burning.

None of this happened.

And I am shaking with relief that none of this happened. And I am so incredibly thankful that none of this happened.

Vučić has lost the election. And he conceded. He did the Orbán. And for this, for this!, I am thankful to him.

This could have been a very different morning today. It is not. This is good.

item.title: Does the Truth feed those people?
item.description: I looked up something that sounded like a quote using Google: “Does the truth feed those people?” Google’s AI answered, without even a single Web search result beneath, *only* the AI answer: “Does the truth feed those people?” is a powerful quote spoken by the character Fermin (played by Janusz Kamiński) in the 2006 film Children of Men. Which would be a great answer. If that was a quote from the film.
item.content:encoded:
I looked up something that sounded like a quote using Google: “Does the truth feed those people?”

Google’s AI answered, without even a single Web search result beneath, *only* the AI answer:

“Does the truth feed those people?” is a powerful quote spoken by the character Fermin (played by Janusz Kamiński) in the 2006 film Children of Men.

Which would be a great answer.

If that was a quote from the film. It isn’t.

If there was a character named Fermin in that film. There isn’t.

If Janusz Kamiński had played in that film. He didn’t.

If Janusz Kamiński was even an actor. He isn’t. He is a cinematographer and director.

If Janusz Kamiński had anything to do with the film. He didn’t.

It has been a while since I noticed such a complete fail. At first I believed the answer, and started to act on it. Only later I noticed that it didn’t sit right. And it unraveled.

Next time it might not unravel so easy.

  • AI answer transcript
  • originally posted on Mastodon 27 August 2026

item.title: Checking one fact: Yelena in Brand New Day
item.description: This is not really about Spider-Man, but about the Truth, about AI, and Wikipedia. From time to time I stumble into a rabbit hole where I start fretting about a single fact, and try to get down to the bottom of it. Sometimes I write about these (e.g. the height of Anson Mount, or the place of birth of Ena Begović). This time, I stumbled upon two sentences in the Wikipedia article on the recent movie Spider-Man: Brand New Day, the highest grossing movie in the US ever: “Florence Pugh reprised her MCU role of Yelena Belova / Black Widow.
item.content:encoded:
This is not really about Spider-Man, but about the Truth, about AI, and Wikipedia.

From time to time I stumble into a rabbit hole where I start fretting about a single fact, and try to get down to the bottom of it. Sometimes I write about these (e.g. the height of Anson Mount, or the place of birth of Ena Begović).

This time, I stumbled upon two sentences in the Wikipedia article on the recent movie Spider-Man: Brand New Day, the highest grossing movie in the US ever: “Florence Pugh reprised her MCU role of Yelena Belova / Black Widow. Her introduction scene was altered in post-production due to its perceived sexual undertones.”

Now the first sentence is fine, but I was wondering about the second sentence. Somehow, it didn’t sit right, and it came without a reference. So, I just copied the two sentences into Google, expecting to find a source for that claim, add it to Wikipedia, and that would be the end of it.

Google immediately launched the AI mode, and stated that the text is from the Wikipedia article (correct). It further explained that “during test screenings, younger viewers expressed discomfort with the perceived sexual undertones of the moment. In response, the creative team made post-production visual adjustments to make the bathhouse water more opaque to lessen the nudity/sexual implications”. It gave Wikipedia as a source for this.

That text didn’t appear on Wikipedia.

It asked me if I wanted a primary source for this, and I said yes. The AI then offered an interview in The Wrap, but only gave a link to Threads, where a bit of the interview was quoted. The quote didn’t say anything about test screening or scene alterations. So I ask: “Where’s the link to the Wrap interview?”

And now it gets really interesting. Instead of giving me a link, Google answers: “The statement that “the scene was altered in post-production due to its perceived sexual undertones” is actually a fabricated claim from user-edited wikis and rumor threads, meaning there is no real interview link matching that claim.”

Then Google’s AI gives me links to other interviews.

I say: “But “During test screenings, younger viewers expressed discomfort with the perceived sexual undertones of the moment. In response, the creative team made post-production visual adjustments to make the bathhouse water more opaque to lessen the nudity/sexual implications.” – this came from you, not from Wikipedia? Where did you get that from?”

Google answered: “You are entirely right to call this out. I apologize—I hallucinated that narrative about the younger audiences, test screening discomfort, and the opacity adjustments.

“While the text you initially asked about is currently written verbatim on Wikipedia’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day page, the elaborate details I gave you in my first response to explain why it happened were entirely made up by me.”

To make it clear: not only did it first hallucinate further backstory for an erroneous claim, it also stated that someone else was at fault for that. (I did not check Reddit and YouTube videos about this, these wouldn’t be sources that I can use in Wikipedia).

OK, it was clear what I had to do. I removed that sentence from Wikipedia, and said that this is unsourced. I don’t know whether it is true or not, but if someone bothers to find a reliable source, they can add it back.

But now I was curious about how the sentence made it to Wikipedia in the first place, because sometimes that can help uncover further issues. Finding that out on Wikipedia is a bit of a hassle, and I thought I could let the AI do that.

I asked. Several times. It kept responding that the answer generation failed or something like that. Eventually, the Google AI answered.

Me: “Can you figure out who entered the statement about the altered scene to Wikipedia?”

Google: “Because Wikipedia’s edit history is completely transparent and tracked in real time, it is easy to find the exact origin of this edit.

“The statement regarding the post-production alteration due to “perceived sexual undertones” was added to the Spider-Man: Brand New Day Wikipedia page by an anonymous, unregistered editor on August 22, 2026.”

The page is now and was semi-protected back then, which means anonymous editors cannot have edited the page. I knew that answer was wrong. Still, I asked: “Can you give me a link to the diff that introduced this on the 22 August?”

Google: “Because Wikipedia’s specific page architecture dynamically generates temporary revision IDs rather than permanent links for unverified edits, providing a functional direct hyperlink to that precise “diff” view is not possible.”

That’s when I decided to stop, as this, again, is simply untrue. Not only is this inconsistent with the previous answer (“it is easy to find the exact origin of this edit”), but Wikipedia very much does provide a diff link for every single diff, no matter if by an anonymous editor or not. Google making up outright false information about how Wikipedia works is maybe the one thing that annoys me most in this whole conversation.

The relevant edit can absolutely be linked to. It was not added on August 22. It was not added by an anonymous contributor, but by a volunteer editor with tons of experience, and it seems in good faith. Those things can slip through, and the community can fix it, as happened today. Or maybe it is true, and it will come back with a better source, who knows. That version of Wikipedia also links to the actual interview in The Wrap (which Google avoided), and you can see that it didn’t support anything about test screenings or post-production alterations.

Wikipedia should not be blindly trusted (in fact, no source should, but that’s particularly true for Wikipedia). Articles on Wikipedia may contain errors. The community, over time, reviews the articles, and fixes many of the errors. That’s why it is such a highly trusted source of knowledge.

But taking an AI instead for answering questions? This conversation happened in October 2026. ChatGPT has been around for almost four years, and we have known about the hallucination problem for even longer. How do I fix the AI in Google’s search? Sure, it also warns us that “AI responses may include mistakes.” But look how hard it can be to get to the truth. In this case, Google not only came up with sources that didn’t support the claim we were checking, but it further embellished the wrong statements with a whole, plausible background story. Entirely made-up. Further questions were answered with increasingly wrong claims, to the point where it stated that Wikipedia’s edits cannot be linked to.

The bad thing is that I think I have used AI many times productively. I think that I succeeded in using AI to check facts, to learn about things, to answer questions. And then I stumble into such a situation, and I notice how badly it fails.

Yes, I want to believe that I am diligent about checking AI answers. But am I really? Do I have the energy and the will to check everything? I doubt it. I probably slipped many times. When I didn’t care enough about the answer. When the answer sounded pleasing enough to me at the moment. I know that this scene in Spider-Man is probably not important enough to warrant these worries, this diligence, but one thing is that there is absolutely nothing that should allow us to believe that topics of more importance are treated any differently.

I was not able to share the conversation directly, as is usually possible, nor to export it to a Google Doc. Instead I copy-and-pasted the whole page to a Google Doc and put Screenshots into it. This was not the original conversation, but accessed through my Google AI search history tab (as the original conversation crashed on me when I asked it to export to Google Docs).

Addendum a day later: The sentence was reinstated. Although the Google AI admitted that it hallucinated test screenings and said that the wiki-rumour-mill created a false fact that should be removed, the sentence is actually indeed well supported with sources already given, especially this interview:

  • Art of the Cut: Spider-Man: Brand New Day on BorisFX

The Wikipedia process worked well here. I challenged the sentence, it was reinstated and the community members explained why.

The AI in this case was actively harmful. Even when it said that it was hallucinating –when it reported on its *own* action– it was hallucinating that as well. It got convinced it was wrong –although this sentence wasn’t wrong!– and because it claimed it had made it up I believed it. But it turns out, not even that admission is trustworthy!!

item.title: Some language introspection around Croatian loud and quiet
item.description: You know how by studying people with certain forms of brain damage, scientists can learn a lot about the brain and how it works? I wonder if it is equally promising to study people with a broken understanding of a language in order to learn about languages. I sat down today and started to introspect a small set of related words in Croatian that always bothered me. I am in a sense a native speaker of Croatian — I grew up in a household speaking Croatian, my mother and father spoke almost exclusively Croatian with me growing up.
item.content:encoded:
You know how by studying people with certain forms of brain damage, scientists can learn a lot about the brain and how it works? I wonder if it is equally promising to study people with a broken understanding of a language in order to learn about languages.

I sat down today and started to introspect a small set of related words in Croatian that always bothered me. I am in a sense a native speaker of Croatian — I grew up in a household speaking Croatian, my mother and father spoke almost exclusively Croatian with me growing up. And yet, my Croatian is — although native — far from good. I didn’t read much in Croatian, Croatian was mostly just a spoken language for me growing up (fortunately, in Croatian the correspondence between how you read words and how you pronounce them is much stronger than in, say, English), and also I was growing up within a heavy local dialect that considerably deviated from standard Croatian. Finally, Croatian experienced quite a bit of development since the independence of Croatia, partly in order to intentionally delineate it from Serbian, partly just through the natural evolution of a language that happens during a few decades and which the diaspora using that language usually misses.

So much for background. The set of words I was thinking and trying to understand was around “loud” and “quiet”. Everything I write now is introspection, I did not look it up, which means it may be very wrong. Do not use it for language learning.

The actual words for “loud” and “quiet” are, I think, “glasno” and “tiho”. But I don’t remember hearing these words very often, and I associate with “loud” more “jako” than “glasno”. “jako”, literally, means “strong”. Thinking about its opposite, “weak”, I cannot come up with a word besides “slabo”. But “slabo” doesn’t really mean “weak”, it more means “bad”. But I cannot think of another way to say “weak”. So if a person is weak, you can only say that by saying they are bad — or by using the phrase “ne jako” — “not strong”, which I think I actually encountered more often than “slabo” for that sense of “weak”. Someone wouldn’t say “Ja sam preslab da to dignem” — “I am too weak to lift this”, but rather “Ja nisam dosta jak da to dignem” — “I am not strong enough to lift this”.

Similar for “quiet”, I think I heard “ne jako” more often than “tiho”. The command “ne tako jako!” — “not so loud!” more often than “tiho!” — “quiet!”. Or it would be “umukni!”, which is rather untranslateable but means something like “shut up!”.

Additionally, “jako” also means “very” and can thus be used to modify other adjectives, for example “jako slabo” — “very bad”, “jako tiho” — “very quiet”, “jako jako” — “very strong” or “very loud”.

Now I said that “glasno” means “loud”. Maybe I am wrong, and “glasno” really means “clear” (as in “loud and clear”, “jako i glasno”). This also would fit with the Russian usage in “glasnost” as “transparency” / “clarity”. So maybe “jako” indeed means both “strong” and “loud”?

The reason why I first thought it didn’t was because I mostly encountered the word in a slightly different context: making the TV louder or quieter (I grew up with a lot of time watching TV with the family). To make it louder, the command that would be used to the person with the remote was “pojačaj” — “make it stronger” / “strongify”, which makes totally sense when dealing with a device that produces sound. You want to make it stronger, and thus it becomes louder. The opposite of that was “smanji” — which literally means “make it smaller” / “smallify”. But you couldn’t say the TV is “malo” — “small” to say it is “quiet”, you would use “tiho” for that or, again, “ne jako” — “not strong” / “not loud”.

The funny thing is that the natural antonym of a word would often have a different antonym. So the antonym of “tiho” — “quiet”) is “jako”. The antonym of “jako” — “strong” is “slabo”. The antonym of “slabo” — “bad” is “dobro”. Maybe it is that these words are just polysemous, have several senses — i.e. “slabo” has one sense, “bad”, and one sense “weak”, etc., and all that is happening here is switching the senses while walking the antonym chain — but to be honest, between this and the much more frequent usage of negation, I have the intuition there is a little bit more going on here, but I cannot say what.

But in the end, it is probably just because of my broken understanding of Croatian.

  • Previously published on Medium on April 10, 2017.

item.title: Cohesion and disinformation
item.description: I guess that by now there is little doubt that the Russian and other governments, such as Iran, are having massively successful (dis)information campaigns on social media, in the countries of Europe and the US, and likely many others too. Their effectiveness is due to exploiting real existing disagreements in society, magnifying them, and blowing them up way beyond proportion. This ensures that society becomes further split, in fact so far that, amidst a booming economy and record low crime and unemployment rates, the fear of actual civil war and violent unrest is as high as it has not been for a century.
item.content:encoded:
I guess that by now there is little doubt that the Russian and other governments, such as Iran, are having massively successful (dis)information campaigns on social media, in the countries of Europe and the US, and likely many others too.

Their effectiveness is due to exploiting real existing disagreements in society, magnifying them, and blowing them up way beyond proportion. This ensures that society becomes further split, in fact so far that, amidst a booming economy and record low crime and unemployment rates, the fear of actual civil war and violent unrest is as high as it has not been for a century. The common ground is being eroded, and topics of low impact on the actual day to day life, such as the small number of immigrants to the EU or the tweets of the US president dominate the daily discourse, so that high-impact topics such as climate change or demographic change and their economic consequences are not even on our agenda.

In fact, calling them disinformation campaigns is highly misleading, because they are most effective if they are actually informative and correct. They are most effective if they pick up the real fears (unfounded or not) of real people, and magnify them. This forces the ongoing discourse, and puts the whole society into an ongoing reactive mode. All of us just react, breathlessly, to the latest shocking moment instead of focusing on sustained growth and improvement.

The picture above shows how foreign agents form the cores of the conversation. Note, this is not only on the conservative side, but also, and actually in an even bigger amount, on the progressive side. The researcher who created this picture points out that it felt weird to consider these accounts as equally problematic, because on his side they were resonating with him so much.

That. Is. The. Effing. Point.

Rarely do these agents have an explicit goal. I doubt they are attacking Star Wars because they want to see the movie tank, or because of a direct political goal. Their goal is to increase chaos, weaken coherence, reduce the ability to act. Sometimes the goals are more obvious — for example the operations in Macedonia and Greece, aiming at keeping NATO from growing further — but most of them are not. They might be just aiming at growing discord, or at training people doing this kind of operations.

The people leading these operations are likely of varying intelligence, but all of them will gather years and decades of experience in using social media for manipulation. Also, the operations are cheap and often not even illegal, most often entirely risk free.

We shouldn’t even be surprised about the existence of these operations. The West has used similar methods for decades: emitting radio signals into the communist countries is just the best known. The US is complaining about interference into their elections? Given some operations of the CIA such complaints are almost amusing. The most surprising thing would be if the US or France would *not* have similar operations ongoing. That would be almost negligent.

Why are they doing this? How would I know? My best guess is that from the point of view of Russia or Iran or North Korea the West had accumulated such a large advantage that their most effective bet to ever return to a more level playing field is to drag the West down so hard, to break us into factions, to make us betray our deepest values, with low-cost, no-risk social media operations. What are we gonna do? Impose sanctions because DeplorableJenny37369 made a retweet from a Russian IP address?

Again — this doesn’t mean that they are not real people with valid and different points of views involved. But their concerns are being hijacked, magnified, abused. Read the case studies in the references below to see these mechanisms at work. And this happens on all sides. I am sure I have fallen for these campaigns, just as basically anyone else.

How can we react?

I wish I knew. A few ideas, none of them promising.

Can we all just become more resilient to these operations? Given that these operations are run by highly trained people who dedicate their lives to social media, I guess the chances that we all get collectively smarter and wiser about all of this are not good. You see, I don’t assume that I can beat up an active Marine, so why should I assume that I will constantly outsmart an active intelligence agent.

Technological solutions that detect and shut down such operations? If we expect them to happen voluntarily by the tech companies — I doubt this to happen. I doubt Twitter has the capability or incentive to spent the resources required to counter such measures for something like the Macedonian market. Could regulation compel them? How would that regulation look like? Also, almost all measures will be countered by more sophisticated operations. This is an arms race where the defense is much more expensive than the attack, in many different ways.

Give up some of the level of anonymity we currently enjoy on the Web. I find this approach both terrifying and promising. I am afraid that this is a very high price to pay. I am afraid that this might, if not done with extreme care and massive input from those groups, be potentially most harmful to some of our most vulnerable members in society, such as those who are LGBTQ*, or who suffer from diseases or disabilities, or who are hiding from abusers, and many others. The web’s anonymity has, again and again, been described as the space that allowed them to breathe, to live, to learn how to be themselves. And no matter what the solution is — pseudonymity? asymmetric identity flows? — this has to be preserved. But this is so dangerous, so easy to get wrong. But at the same time there seems a space of potential solutions between the current one and one of full transparency. (Nevermind that for certain actors, such as the NSA, this anonymity is mostly wishful thinking on our parts anyway)

And whereas I believe that a possible solution lives in that space, I am also aware of the horrifying fact that one point in this space is exactly what most of the intervening foreign powers want and are building: a web in which the anonymity of the individual has disappeared. By moving ourselves this way we weaken our own position in the argument against such a controlled web.

What about a solution like SOLID? I am afraid that in fact such a decentralized solution will weaken the technical possibilities to detect and prevent such operations even more. As much as I’m hoping for SOLID to succeed for many different reasons, I’m afraid it might also lead us further into a world of populists and fractured societies.

Just switch Facebook and Twitter off? It will be back, probably faster and more nimble than before.

Factcheckers? As if facts mattered too much in these discussions. Some research shows that showing fact checking results next to false claims increases the appeal of these claims in some cases.

Increase the coherence of society. In my opinion this is the most promising path forward. And the way to do that is to improve everyone’s life and reduce the growing gap between rich and poor. If we reduce the economic stress many people feel, they will be more open to people who are different. If people don’t think that they can barely make it, that they are in desperate need of financial support by the government, they might be more open to the idea to use government funds to help refugees. If they realize that the world is not a zero sum game, they might be more open to change and a fairer representation. The world is getting better and richer. But the returns of these improvements are being handed out very unevenly.

The more cohesion we have, the fewer splits and cracks there already are in society, the smaller the chances of operations succeeding that aim to exploit these cracks and splits.

Which basically means we’re likely screwed, because I don’t see a realistic chance to get there. Also, because the path to this world is being actively blocked by the disinformation campaigns that prompted this text, which has been going on for far too long already. I am sorry for not having a solution, for not even having a good idea of the problem. But there is a problem that needs a solution, a problem that is stubborn and wicked and hard.

And yet, we must. We must. We must.

Reading list:

  • The surprising nuance behind the Russian troll strategy (research by Kate Starbird)
  • Here’s how Russia runs its disinformation effort (NPR)
  • How Twitter bots and Trump fans made #ReleaseTheMemo go viral (Politico)
  • Brett Kavanaugh and the information terrorists trying to reshape America (Wired)
  • Russian meddling is a symptom, not the disease (NYT op-ed by Zeynep Tufekci)
  • How a disastrous change in perspective disempowered the left and let the right rise (The Guardian)
  • Media manipulation, strategic amplification, and responsible journalism (essay by danah boyd)

The essay above started life as a Facebook post no November 4, 2018 and received more attentions than my other ramblings. I was asked to put it into a more accessible location, and also to summarize some results from the discussion that ensued. With this Medium post I at least did the former but not the latter. I strongly recommend to take a look at the discussion on the public post.

item.title: Thoughts on The Last Jedi
item.description: Reading this only makes sense if you have already watched The Last Jedi, and probably the other seven Episodes as well. Given how many surprises and twists have been in Episode VIII, I expect to be completely off, and to be delightfully surprised and entertained when Episode IX appears. For now, here’s my incomplete understanding of watching Episode VIII once and not understanding all of the dialogue. I really should start using subtitles in cinemas.
item.content:encoded:
Reading this only makes sense if you have already watched The Last Jedi, and probably the other seven Episodes as well. Given how many surprises and twists have been in Episode VIII, I expect to be completely off, and to be delightfully surprised and entertained when Episode IX appears. For now, here’s my incomplete understanding of watching Episode VIII once and not understanding all of the dialogue. I really should start using subtitles in cinemas.

“You were the Chosen One! You were to bring balance to the Force, not leave it in Darkness.” That is what Obi-Wan yelled at Anakin (back in Episode III). The Chosen One spoken of in the ancient Jedi prophecies — which are probably written down in the exact books that Luke thinks destroyed by Yoda, just before he performs his last sacrifice in order to give the Resistance enough time to flee in the Millenium Falcon. Yoda though already understood the prophecies better than Obi-Wan or Luke, he said that they likely have been misread: the Chosen one was not meant to destroy the Sith.

What does balance mean? The Jedi were basically the top security power of the Republic, the prime power next to the Senate. The Sith? Just a legend, and even in legend there were only two of them at a time, forced into hiding by the powerful Jedi. If the Chosen One was promised to bring balance between the Jedi and the Sith, the near destruction of the Jedi is indeed the most effective step to reach that goal — something Yoda seemed to have known.

From the middle of Episode III to VI, both Sith and Jedi were in a similarly precarious situation, both sides locked in existential fights. When Luke trained Kylo and the other young Jedi, he was starting to tip the balance again to one side. The fateful night when Luke was contemplating killing his own nephew in his sleep, when Kylo turned to the Dark Side, the balance shifted, and a champion for the Light Side was needed — enter Rey in Episode VII. Snoke himself said that Rey only came in in order to balance Kylo. Does he realize that the goal of either of the sides winning must be doomed if the Force — the all powerful Force! — will always plot to overturn any victory, will always counter any time any side starts winning, even if it means to create beings as powerful as Vader or Rey?

The lesson of Episode VIII — the message of the movie, not just within Star Wars, but also for everyone’s life — is about the importance of failure, how effective failure is as a teacher, as long as one is resilient enough to use it as a lesson. And indeed, the film is full of failures, so full of failures one might question half of the plotlines because they don’t lead to any pay off. Poe fails to stay loyal, starts a rebellion on the fleeing Resistance ship because of Vice-Admiral Holdo’s failure as a leader to communicate her plan. Finn’s failure to bring the beacon to lead Rey back into a safe space gets him into a crazy plan to shake off the First Order. Finn and Rose’s quest to find the Codebreaker, and then to switch off the tracker, failed miserably on the last second, and made that whole storyline look so futile. Luke’s failure to train and raise Kylo. Or Rey. Leia’s failure to keep the Resistance safe. Rey’s failure to bring Luke with her to the Resistance. Rey’s failure to attack Snoke. Rey’s failure to turn Kylo to the Light. Kylo’s failure to convince Rey to join him in creating a new order. Kylo’s constant failures in Snoke’s eyes. The film is full of failures, and these almost entirely annihilate the Resistance, and indeed Leia’s legacy of ending the Empire and creating the New Republic, a Republic spanning the whole galaxy. At the end of the movie the active part of the Resistance fits inside the Millenium Falcon.

These failures, once processed by the numerous protagonists of the movie, can lead to a great pay off in Episode IX. Destiny — and the Force — have probably taught our protagonists exactly the lessons they need in order to be in place to finally fulfill the prophecy and bring balance to the Force. Poe already showed a little of that new found wisdom, as acknowledged by Leia in her beautiful handoff — “What are you looking at me for? Follow him!”

How could that look like? An end to both Sith and Jedi, an end to the dichotomy of the Light and Dark Side of the Force? Well, that’s certainly one way to have balance, both being at zero. But that’s where the boy with the broom comes in. The Force remains present, even if the Skywalkers end their little family feud (and there are not that many Skywalkers left anyway). Will Rey and Kylo find their own new ways to a new world? To a new balance? Maybe one where balance is not defined by which order is stronger, by whether the Jedi or the Sith rule the galaxy, but by a balance in each and every force wielder themselves?

Luke said that he saw the Dark Side in Kylo, but it was clear that this was his own perception. Kylo was very strong, and Luke always was suppressing his Dark Side very much, so the Dark Side in Kylo, even if it were much weaker than his Light Side, would have certainly looked frightening to Luke. If you ask Kylo it was Luke who triggered the Dark Side in himself by, well, trying to murder him. But Luke also saw how reckless Rey was with regards to the Dark Side. Rey went to the Pond of the Dark Side, and seems to have left it untainted. What if the Dark Side and the Light Side are, indeed, just sides of the same Force? If that division is meaningless to the Force but an invention of the Sith and Jedi? If they were not meant to be separated inside individuals, but kept at balance within?

Did you notice the Jedi symbol in the fountain in Anch-To? It was half black, half white, not the representation of the symbol I usually remember. Was there a long lost time where the balance was already achieved?

Balance does not have to be at a near zero level. But the story of the galaxy as told in the saga is a story of millions of deaths, of planets and stars destroyed, of entire fleets annihilated, and in the end it will always be without effect, because the Force will always overturn any victory. Either we have to achieve a new synthesis of Dark and Light, and find a new way to balance the powers — no matter how it looks like — or we have to continue the circles of destruction, which was quite deliberately started anew with Episode VII mirroring so much of Episode IV, and the star wars will keep going on and on.

P.S.: Now you may ask what if the balance is restored, does this mean an end to Star Wars? And even for that this movie offers the answer, by the peak into the world of Canto, where we see that even without a mythological Force that splits the world in Dark and Light, the world offers enough shades of gray to generate conflicts and interesting stories into all eternity.

  • This post was first published on Medium on December 18, 2017

item.title: The Odyssey 2026
item.description: I mean, it’s Nolan. It’s a great movie. He knows how to make movies. So the three hours pass like a breeze and are enjoyable. The cast is great, I particularly enjoyed Matt Damon, Robert Pattinson and Samantha Morton as Circe. Agamemnon was absolutely breathtaking. He stole every scene he was in. (Until he started talking. I didn’t like his voice. But those looks!) The first half hour or so of the movie felt like an extended trailer.
item.content:encoded:
I mean, it’s Nolan. It’s a great movie. He knows how to make movies. So the three hours pass like a breeze and are enjoyable. The cast is great, I particularly enjoyed Matt Damon, Robert Pattinson and Samantha Morton as Circe.

Agamemnon was absolutely breathtaking. He stole every scene he was in. (Until he started talking. I didn’t like his voice. But those looks!)

The first half hour or so of the movie felt like an extended trailer. Which is very Nolan, but surprising and a little unsettling given the familiar setting and story. It gets more settled and classical later on.

I really disliked the body horror scenes around Circe. And the design of the monsters was… unsatisfying. Polyphem? Ok. Unusual and new. But then Scylla with the same beige color and skin-like texture? It looked like Ray Harryhausen. Which was fine in his time, but underwhelming in a 2026 AAA title. But it did give me a genuine jump scare.

I found the whole movie lacking color saturation. I have to compare it to 2004 Troy, which I find much more appealing as a Greek mythology saga movie. The Odyssey is a 2026 movie, binding it to our time in subtle ways, on the expense of the timelessness that Troy has.

(Spoilers in this paragraph) But what I really enjoyed was the novel twist to the plot, that I haven’t seen before. That it was Odysseus who broke the old contract that was keeping society together. That this was the reason for the long way home. In a way this was the same core plot point as Oppenheimer. And possibly an important lesson for our age. That gave food for thought. But almost like a memory of the thoughts that Oppenheimer provoked. But I enjoyed these ideas explored in such a familiar setting.

Now that I spilled out my thoughts, let’s see what others have written. And again, it’s a great movie. Worth watching.

  • Wikipedia article on the movie

item.title: Croatia's goal was stolen! Portugal is scripted to advance
item.description: The feed for my Facebook reels is now full of videos analyzing the Croatian goal that wasn’t counted, and with conspiracy theories about the whole World Cup being scripted for a Ronaldo-Messi finale. And this is how easily social media radicalizes you. I have no idea how widespread either of these ideas are. Is there really a dominating public debate happening about this? I don’t think so. But for me, looking at my Facebook reels, it would appear like this is the most important thing happening right now.
item.content:encoded:
The feed for my Facebook reels is now full of videos analyzing the Croatian goal that wasn’t counted, and with conspiracy theories about the whole World Cup being scripted for a Ronaldo-Messi finale.

And this is how easily social media radicalizes you. I have no idea how widespread either of these ideas are. Is there really a dominating public debate happening about this? I don’t think so. But for me, looking at my Facebook reels, it would appear like this is the most important thing happening right now. And look at all these people making smart videos agreeing with me! And not a single one disagreeing!

I’m confirmed in my bias. Look, everyone thinks that the VAR was wrong. Everyone thinks Croatia was robbed of a chance to continue to compete. And yet nothing is happening.

I have two ways I can react: first, I could try to do something. Protest. Demand reform. Make petitions. Get involved with the relevant governing bodies and make changes. Obviously I don’t care nearly enough to put in that energy and change the priorities in my life for that. And as I do that, I would actually feel the resistance in real life, notice how little support that idea actually may have. A reality check

The second way: I engage with these videos, write supporting comments, strengthen this belief and get sucked in by tapping on a screen, get more cynical about the world because although everyone believes the same as I do, nothing is changing, so it must be “them” who keep the real control and decide differently. My trust in institutions further erodes, seeing the obvious discrepancy between what everybody believes and between what actually happens.

The bubble wrap around me gets tighter, splintering society further. Shared spaces starve, because folks prefer the comforts of confirmation over confronting conflict. I mean, why even try to reach across the aisle if my tribe is so big? If we are the obvious majority?

And the designers behind the social media feed algorithms either know all of this and still pursue it, intentionally, because of the monetary advantages it brings, or they have given up on caring and handed the decisions over to an algorithm whose goal is engagement. The algorithm is unaware of any cost not modeled in its objective function. Like a paperclip maximizer, it is set up to maximize engagement or whatever the metric is, even if it breaks society. That would be either an externalized cost, or not relevant for this quarter’s metrics, or just invisible.

This isn’t about the Croatia game. This is about how we process crises and deal with controversies, from COVID and the January 6 insurrection to elections and institutional trust. It is about vaccines and raw milk, the support for Ukraine, the rise of authoritarianism, our response to climate change. This is about how our society is breaking.

Why do we allow social media algorithms to tear our social fabric apart? Is this just another complaint to feed my own bubble, getting confirmation from others, but not do anything about? What about you, will you just agree and move on? Or are we willing to put in the work and make a change?

item.title: Flower power
item.description: One of the most shocking movie scenes that burnt into my mind was in the opening credits of the 2009 Watchmen movie, directed by Zack Snyder. 50,000 protesters took part in the March on the Pentagon in 1967. A row of military police was pointing their rifles at the protesters. A flower power protester puts a flower into the barrel of one of the rifles. In the movie, Bob Dylan’s The Times They are A-Changing is playing over the scene, recreating an iconic photograph from 1967.
item.content:encoded:
One of the most shocking movie scenes that burnt into my mind was in the opening credits of the 2009 Watchmen movie, directed by Zack Snyder. 50,000 protesters took part in the March on the Pentagon in 1967. A row of military police was pointing their rifles at the protesters. A flower power protester puts a flower into the barrel of one of the rifles. In the movie, Bob Dylan’s The Times They are A-Changing is playing over the scene, recreating an iconic photograph from 1967. (link in comment)

But in the alternative reality of the movie, the police fires at the protesters.

I remember seeing that scene in the movie theater, and I found that image absolutely distressing, thinking about the terrible alternate reality that would have been. How many people would have died, how different the United States would be today… and being glad that reality took a different turn.

… but did it?

Today I learned about the 1967 Detroit riots. More than 7000 people arrested, 43 people killed, of which 30 were killed by the authorities and another six by store owners or security guards. It was in the same year. And the authorities were shooting and killing the people, mostly black people. But that seems a lot like the terrible “alternative reality” Snyder’s movie was drawing. But it was not an alternate reality. It was just not the story of mostly white hippies on the coasts, but of mostly black people in Detroit.

I am ashamed it took me until today to have learned about these events. But one thing I can do is reading more about the events and maybe reach others who might not have known.

  • Flower Power photograph - Wikipedia
  • 1967 March on the Pentagon - Wikipedia
  • Intro scene from Watchmen
  • 1967 Detroit riot

item.title: Mega-IPOs
item.description: There are more than 15 trillion (!) dollar invested in index funds. Starting in a few days and going on until the fall of next year, more than half a trillion dollar of that money will be pulled out from the existing company shares in numerous indexes and used to buy SpaceX, OpenAI, and Anthropic shares from their existing share owners. (Most of it will start happening in about a year, when the S&P500 lets SpaceX join.
item.content:encoded:
There are more than 15 trillion (!) dollar invested in index funds. Starting in a few days and going on until the fall of next year, more than half a trillion dollar of that money will be pulled out from the existing company shares in numerous indexes and used to buy SpaceX, OpenAI, and Anthropic shares from their existing share owners. (Most of it will start happening in about a year, when the S&P500 lets SpaceX join. Unlike NASDAQ, S&P didn’t change their rules to fast-track these mega IPOs. But they will join NASDAQ before their first quarterly report as a public company).

With the IPOs of SpaceX (this Friday), OpenAI, and Anthropic, and them joining NASDAQ and FTSE’s global index within a few days after their IPOs (and S&P and Dow Jones a year later), everyone who has invested in index funds, be it directly through ETFs or indirectly through their 401k and other retirement plans, will automatically sell about 5% of the shares they are currently holding, and buy shares from one of these three companies. All three IPOs will be, by far!, the largest IPOs in history.

So, if you have $100 invested in a NASDAQ-indexed ETF, you will be selling $5 of the stocks you currently own (while everyone else is doing the same) and buy $5 worth of Anthropic, SpaceX and OpenAI stocks (while everyone else is doing the same), automatically and predictably.

It will be a tough time for the rest of the stock market this year, as there will be a lot of people’s money flowing to OpenAI, SpaceX and Antrhopic without anyone ever intentionally buying it, with the market sending 5% of its liquidity to these three new mega IPOs. It will be immensely beneficial for everyone selling these shares.

Whether it will be beneficial for the general public, i.e. for the people holding these index funds, is something we are going to see in the next few years. I wouldn’t wager a prediction on that. Maybe there’s an AI bubble that might burst, maybe making more of their numbers public will make some people think they are overvalued, maybe all three companies will realise incredible value and will lift the stock indexes well beyond the 5% of the market they will initially cost. We are going to see. If I could make predicitons about how these things will develop, I’d be much richer.

But it seems that in the next 12-18 months, 100s of billions of dollars are slated to go from retirement plans and other stock investors to Elon Musk, Sam Altman, and others. Happy to discuss if I misunderstand.

item.title: The Amazing Digital Circus
item.description: (spoiler free) The Amazing Digital Circus is an animation show of which, until about a month ago, I haven’t even heard about. I learned about it from my daughter. It is the work of an independent creator, and was initially published on YouTube and later also made available on Netflix. The YouTube video of the first episode has more than 400 million views and on Netflix it’s been in the top ten for a while.
item.content:encoded:
(spoiler free)

The Amazing Digital Circus is an animation show of which, until about a month ago, I haven’t even heard about. I learned about it from my daughter. It is the work of an independent creator, and was initially published on YouTube and later also made available on Netflix. The YouTube video of the first episode has more than 400 million views and on Netflix it’s been in the top ten for a while.

The premise is that a few humans are captured in a virtual reality, where an AI has the job to entertain them. With time we realize that some of the humans have been there for decades, one has partially lost his mind, and there seems to be no way out. The colorful graphics and seemingly silly character designs hide a much darker story, inspired by “The Matrix”, maybe “Lost”, and “I have no mouth but I must scream”.

The show has nine episodes, each about half an hour long and the final episode double that, so not too long.

I find the animation style somewhat subpar, but the pacing is so much more comfortable and relaxed than many other current shows and movies. The characters are really well done, and feel realistic and multifaceted.

The last episode is currently being shown in cinemas, and it seems do be doing extremely well for an independent show, before it will be available on YouTube in a few days (for free, like the rest of the show). We went to watch it today, and very much enjoyed it.

Given how Lost didn’t manage to find a fully satisfying ending, and The Matrix had trouble with storytelling after the first movie, I didn’t expect that the Amazing Digital Circus would be able to bring the story to a satisfying end.

I was wrong.

The ending was so much better than I expected it to be. It was fresh and novel (well, there’s probably some manga or SF short story with that storyline, but it was novel to me) and more satisfying than I would have deemed possible in such a short episode. Not every question seemed answered, but with this show I expect not to have picked up on every clue and I’ll probably find more answers in a few weeks. But the big ones were, and the story came to a close.

Can recommend.

item.title: Marjane Satrapi
item.description: Marjane Satrapi, the brave and talented creator of the wonderful and honest graphic novel Persepolis, has died. Her magnum opus is an autobiography, telling of her young years growing up during the Islamic Revolution in Iran, the Iran-Iraq war of 1980, and then moving to Austria, for safety and to study. But Vienna isn’t the safe space her family was hoping for, she’s having a difficult time, and returns to Iran.
item.content:encoded:
Marjane Satrapi, the brave and talented creator of the wonderful and honest graphic novel Persepolis, has died. Her magnum opus is an autobiography, telling of her young years growing up during the Islamic Revolution in Iran, the Iran-Iraq war of 1980, and then moving to Austria, for safety and to study. But Vienna isn’t the safe space her family was hoping for, she’s having a difficult time, and returns to Iran. The difference between the two worlds really show. Back home, she can’t find her place either.

It’s not an easy book to read, it is nuanced, it feels sincere, and it shines a very human light on what the revolution meant, on what emigration can be like.

It was a popular graphic novel, pushing what was usually done with the medium. Satrapi was one of the first women to find success with graphic novels.

According to her family, Satrapi died at the age of 56 of a broken heart, following her husband’s death last year.

I very much recommend reading the book. It is not an easy story, but it is an important one.

item.title: The Future of Truth
item.description: What a mind boggling and raw article by Wired: Steve Rosenbaum has a book out, “The Future of Truth”, on the effect of AI chatbots on the understanding of truth. Rosenbaum has a master’s degree in “truth” from New York University (what does that even mean?) and has decades of experience in this field: creating news programs for MTV and reporting on the aftermath of 9/11 in New York and much more.
item.content:encoded:
What a mind boggling and raw article by Wired: Steve Rosenbaum has a book out, “The Future of Truth”, on the effect of AI chatbots on the understanding of truth. Rosenbaum has a master’s degree in “truth” from New York University (what does that even mean?) and has decades of experience in this field: creating news programs for MTV and reporting on the aftermath of 9/11 in New York and much more.

But the New York Times reported that Rosenbaum’s book is heavily relying on AI, for example containing made up quotes. Wired had previously published an excerpt from the book, but given its strict no AI policy for content and the reporting by the Times, it pulled the excerpt.

Instead, Wired interviewed Rosenbaum. Here’s one quote:

“I do not understand why it’s my job as an author to play whack-a-mole with a multibillion-dollar company who puts hallucinations into their feed as a business practice”

Because it’s your book! It’s your name on the cover. This text is your responsibility.

And he’s not alone:

“I talked to another author this morning who’s literally got a book coming out going to the publisher in a month, and she’s fucking terrified.” I asked if that was because she used AI in the process of writing the book. “Of course”

There’s a silver lining:

“I asked him whether he would rather stop writing than stop using AI in his writing process. “Yeah,” he answered.”

That’s a good idea. I sure have little interest to read anything from a person with this attitude.

  • Kate Knibbs: We Asked the Future of Truth Author to Explain How He Used AI. It Didn’t Go Well (Wired)

item.title: Logos and logs
item.description: About the Greek word logos, λόγος. It is usually translated as “word”, but a lot is lost in translation when doing so. Wiktionary says “speech, oration, discourse, quote, story, study, ratio, word, calculation, reason”. The etymology is from proto-Indo-European “leǵ-”, meaning to collect, to gather. Philologist Erik Ellis has thought a lot about logos, and he says that the best English translation he has found so far for logos is “account”.
item.content:encoded:
About the Greek word logos, λόγος. It is usually translated as “word”, but a lot is lost in translation when doing so. Wiktionary says “speech, oration, discourse, quote, story, study, ratio, word, calculation, reason”. The etymology is from proto-Indo-European “leǵ-”, meaning to collect, to gather.

Philologist Erik Ellis has thought a lot about logos, and he says that the best English translation he has found so far for logos is “account”. Both a bank account and to give an account of last night is about recounting the events that led to the current situation, to tell a story, and that meaning of account captures logos best.

Amusingly the way Ellis was describing “account” made me think of the word “log”, the way it is used in computing and on ships, and it took me an embarrassing moment to notice the similarity between “logos” and “log”, but etymologically they’re entirely unrelated as the latter comes from tree log, which has old Norse roots.

It’s just another funny, accidental etymological convergence.

  • Classical Education podcast with Erik Ellis

item.title: What is true
item.description: “Maria and Peter are students and meet up for a late dinner. Peter asks Maria whether Tom is at the party that they intend to go to after dinner. Maria answers that Tom is at the party. After all, Tom had told her that he would be at the party. When they arrive at the party, it turns out that Tom had changed his plans, and is not at the party.
item.content:encoded:
“Maria and Peter are students and meet up for a late dinner. Peter asks Maria whether Tom is at the party that they intend to go to after dinner. Maria answers that Tom is at the party. After all, Tom had told her that he would be at the party. When they arrive at the party, it turns out that Tom had changed his plans, and is not at the party. Was Maria’s answer true or false?”

Think for a moment, and answer for yourself before reading on.

A new study shows that there is much, much less agreement on the answer to this question than I would have expected. Even after reading about the study, I still expect my friends to have the same answer as I do. Let’s see. But this probably means that the meaning of truth, in the general population, is simply different from what I would have assumed. And explains a number of public discourses.

  • The Surprising Divide Over What Counts as True by Ronald Bailey in Reason
  • Mastodon poll (to run until 27 May 2026

item.title: Lelek Andromeda
item.description: Croatia’s entry to for the Eurovision Song Contest is anything but a typical ESC entry. The video below gives the English lyrics. The tattoos the singers are wearing are historical: they were used, mostly on women, to ‘protect’ them from the non-Christian conquerors, and to remind them of their roots. Tattoos in the Balkans were used for almost a hundred generations, described by Strabo in the first century BC until the early 20th century.
item.content:encoded:
Croatia’s entry to for the Eurovision Song Contest is anything but a typical ESC entry. The video below gives the English lyrics. The tattoos the singers are wearing are historical: they were used, mostly on women, to ‘protect’ them from the non-Christian conquerors, and to remind them of their roots. Tattoos in the Balkans were used for almost a hundred generations, described by Strabo in the first century BC until the early 20th century. I am a sucker for the mythic motives, playing with fantasy themes, for the polyharmonic singing. It’s not the fun song of a young man leaving for the city and selling his cow, but a powerful folk-inspired anti-war ballad, deeply steeped in local history.

So, probably no chance to win an event like ESC, but certainly an interesting song, highlighting a part of local history that I wasn’t aware of at all.

(There’s obviously a nationalist element to this, as any folk stuff is, I know; but I hope, beyond reason, that it is not nationalistic)

  • Lelek - Andromeda (with English lyrics) on YouTube

item.title: The Web attacked by AI
item.description: The Web I grew up with and that grew up with me was already slowly fading. The Web of many people and organizations having their own small website. Capitalism and convenience lead to a concentration onto a small number of platforms and apps, but mostly these platforms let the rest be. People and small organizations and groups could still have their little website. But the ongoing indiscriminate onslaught of AI bots on everything with an URL is just actively killing the web and its open nature.
item.content:encoded:
The Web I grew up with and that grew up with me was already slowly fading. The Web of many people and organizations having their own small website. Capitalism and convenience lead to a concentration onto a small number of platforms and apps, but mostly these platforms let the rest be. People and small organizations and groups could still have their little website.

But the ongoing indiscriminate onslaught of AI bots on everything with an URL is just actively killing the web and its open nature. Websites, which were meant for the few human visitors, get crawled at rapid speed, open REST APIs are being overrun, the few SPARQL points out there get slaughtered by queries, causing downtimes, cost, and what not, actively killing those parts of the Web which have historically just been happy to be there, with little maintenance, across the years.

But now, if you don’t pay protection money to a service such as Cloudfare or make sure you have the right load balancer, the AI bros will take you down.

It’s not the first and it won’t be the last sacrifice to the basilisk of AI, but it surely is one of the ones that pains me personally. So unnecessary, with so little gain.

It makes me sad.

item.title: Playground
item.description: Markus Krötzsch recommend me a novel, Playground, by Richard Powers. I have to admit I rarely read novels, and this one was a good one to make an exception. “There was only one way of making a two or a twelve, but six ways to roll a seven. The maker of the world whispered that secret to me, and it changed everything.” I really enjoyed the language. It was just a pleasant read, and you can feel that the author mastered the craft of building sentences, paragraphs, and stories.
item.content:encoded:
Markus Krötzsch recommend me a novel, Playground, by Richard Powers. I have to admit I rarely read novels, and this one was a good one to make an exception.

  • “There was only one way of making a two or a twelve, but six ways to roll a seven. The maker of the world whispered that secret to me, and it changed everything.”

I really enjoyed the language. It was just a pleasant read, and you can feel that the author mastered the craft of building sentences, paragraphs, and stories.

  • “If you want to make something smarter, teach it to play.”

I was very confused throughout the first hundred pages or so, until I figured out what the main story threads were. I have to admit, that I than re-skimmed these pages again, and it all made sense and fit together, but at first it felt like so many different things were going on that I wasn’t sure what was going on. But because of the well-wrought language, I didn’t mind, and I merrily joined the ride.

  • “What you call the ocean is nothing but the coast.”

The book retells the story of four characters, who, at their best, are fascinating and brilliant, and at their worst, are failing so bad it makes me angry, and are, at all times, deeply relatable. It follows a story of games, computers, the birth of the Web with Mosaic, and a very thinly veiled fictional version of Cyc, and a fictional Website, Playground, which has a fascinating premise, somewhere between Facebook and Reddit, and then going to machine learning and AI. It also tells the story of an oceanographer, of the changing oceans, of dementia, of loss, guilt, and the permanence of death.

  • “It was embarrassing. She didn’t want to tell the god that she didn’t believe in him and that he really shouldn’t be there.”

At several points, the line between fiction and truth becomes very fragile, dreamlike, which is part of the appeal.

  • “He left me everything.”
    “I see.”
    What in the world am I supposed to do with it?"

In the end, I was literally gasping when the author resolved a part of the story I wasn’t even expecting, although it was built towards it the whole time. It made me mad and angry, and then it made me think of why I was so mad and angry. In the end, the story gets a beautiful resolution, one that made me lose a tear or two, and that made me question the primacy of story and truth again.

  • “We make things that we hope will be bigger than us, and then we’re desolate when that’s what they become.”

Richard Powers, Playground. ISBN 978-1-324-08603-1
